units.translation: For if you had been slain beneath Ilium, you would have had a tomb heaped high with earth.
You would not be easy to bear, if you were faring well.
For if we should fare well, the credit is the god's; but if, on the other hand—which may it not happen—misfortune should befall, Eteocles alone would be much sung throughout the city.
For if night should fall upon the eyes of the dead—it would be so.
For if they should succeed—then utterly destroyed and most miserably would they perish.
As if the Greeks would escape an evil fate—it was set before them all to be deprived of their heads.
I will come bringing a libation cake—I know it is for deeds already done, but for the future, if anything better might be.
Not even if I should speak for ten days in succession could I satisfy you.
Unless you march to the land of the Greeks.
If the army should come without offense to the gods, it might turn back—if it should not encounter unforeseen evils.
And the danger to you beneath Ilium, whether the people's voice in anarchy might cast down the council.
You would be persuaded if you should persuade.
You would rejoice if you should rejoice.
But if there should be enough of these toils, we would accept it.
You might speak, if you have anything better than these.
I would learn, if someone should speak a clear word.
Uttering pains as goads to my heart, unless I should do something to those responsible.
If we should delay with the shout.
It would be well for us, my children, if they were hated by you and the gods.
You would weep, if you should touch.
Nor does anyone die from many wounds in the chest, unless the end of life should coincide.
If anyone fell into sickness, there was no remedy at all.
And if he should not wish, a fiery thunderbolt from Zeus to come.
But if we should do everything as we do (thus I corrected the faulty 'I would do'), I am confident.
But if indeed the necessity of this fortune weighs down, great is the gratitude of the ancient wealthy masters.
For if I should speak of the toils and the hard lodgings—the cramped and ill-strewn quarters—what part of the day did we not have groaning, not obtaining?
And if someone should speak of the bird-killing winter
Why is it necessary to lament these things?
Not even if an army greater than the Median
Not even if the Median army should be numerous
The ruling hand of the people, wherever it prevails
Whether those fighting with us are more, or few
Lest the people ever say, if something should not turn out such
If the matter should be accomplished perfectly.
Terrible is the wrath of the suppliant's protector, if I willingly betray them.
For the mind is female; but if not, he will soon know.
But if not, you will be without honor among those who feast well.
But if not, we will come.
When, if not now, shall we cling to prayers?
Never except as one who will die with you.
Even if he is too talkative.
Even if you groan in evils, nevertheless.
Even if he is outside the door, nevertheless.
Even if I do not trust.
You will see, even if any other of mortals has sinned.
For if he had sent me beneath the earth—to boundless Tartarus.
If you would grant me, who ask, a light fulfillment.
If a god should grant (thus Schuetz corrected for 'of Zeus') well and truly.
Consider now, if these things seem helpful to you.
Soon we shall know where the tokens lead, if the gold-wrought letters will bring him down.
But if truly, who knows?
And I learn about Menelaus, whether he is returning home.
